airfield_clock.Tarawa: Emergency/garrison fighter use begins about 1-2 Dec from repaired existing surfaces; major permanent fighter-strip/base work continues through Dec. Bomber/staging capability becomes materially useful around 19-23 Dec. Branch secure date does not create a month delay because historical Seabee construction itself largely started at the end of Nov.
airfield_clock.Abemama: Low-resistance development broadly historical: fighter strip useful ~10-13 Dec, bomber extension ~21 Dec. No GALVANIC battle-delay is imposed here.
airfield_clock.Makin: Construction start shifts only several days; fighters/light/medium aircraft become increasingly useful in late Dec and Jan. Heavy-bomber basing remains less attractive than Tarawa/Abemama because of foundation/field characteristics.

Gilbert_forward_air_1944_01_15.roles: fighters/base defense; B-24/B-25/A-24 Marshall pressure; PBY/PBM/PB4Y/PV reconnaissance, ASW and rescue. Not all are same-day strike aircraft.
Gilbert_forward_air_1944_01_15.pressure: Mili/Jaluit receive frequent southern pressure; Taroa/Wotje/Kwajalein require selected long-range heavy/photo missions until carrier arrival.

carrier_surface_regen.Independence: campaign-out; not a Dec/early-Jan offensive deck
carrier_surface_regen.Lexington_CV16: heavy mission-kill/repair; not available for a historical automatic 4-Dec mass Marshall raid
carrier_surface_regen.unnamed_DD_loss: one outer-screen destroyer from 26/27 Nov remains removed; hull identity still open
carrier_surface_regen.4_Dec_rule: Historical mass Kwajalein/Roi raid is not centered. Fast carriers prioritize recovery, cover and reorganization while land-based/photo pressure grows.

post_Tarawa_learning.accepted: more photographic/submarine reconnaissance, more deliberate obstacle/reef intelligence, larger bombardment ammunition allowance, more close-support DD/landing craft/engineers, stronger beach traffic control, repeated reattack of supposedly neutralized positions
post_Tarawa_learning.not_omniscient: US cannot infer hidden Japan-wide productivity or exact next-island layout; damage assessment can still be optimistic and local C2 friction persists
post_Tarawa_learning.bombardment_efficiency_rule: More shells are useful mainly because targets can be re-engaged; 2-3x ammunition does not create 2-3x destructive effect. Smoke/dust, target identification, firing sectors and landing safety remain caps.
post_Tarawa_learning.landing_craft_congestion: More LVT/LST/engineer assets raise robustness but reef lanes, wave control, beach exits, refueling and wreck removal become throughput bottlenecks. Reserve grows faster than simultaneous useful frontage.
post_Tarawa_learning.destroyer_tradeoff: DD assigned to direct-fire reduction cannot simultaneously perform outer SG picket/ASW/transport screen; Japanese submarines and Type-93 raid make this trade real.
post_Tarawa_learning.carrier_tradeoff: Four Japanese first-line carrier decks and surviving submarines force a real CAP/search/anti-carrier reserve. Extra island-suppression sorties are not free.

planning_state_1944_01_15.Kwajalein_direct: still the centered strategic option, roughly 55-65% planning weight
planning_state_1944_01_15.outer_island_first: roughly 30-40%; Tarawa losses strengthen caution, but attacking Taroa/Wotje/Mili individually would expose the fleet longer to the same Japanese network
planning_state_1944_01_15.date: No final D-Day is fixed in this closeout. Assault transport availability, fast-carrier repair/regeneration, reconnaissance and the late-Jan Japanese fleet picture remain gates.
planning_state_1944_01_15.resource_constraint: Two-division direct assault plus heavier bombardment/support package strains assault transports, LVT maintenance, oiler/escort cycles and command bandwidth; this can delay or deconflict tasks rather than simply multiply combat power.
